items.followUp: Define isotopes and name the three isotopes of oxygen, giving their mass numbers.

rubric.why: Defines isotopes by what they share and how they differ.
rubric.how: Award for stating that isotopes have the same atomic number (or number of protons) but different mass numbers (or numbers of neutrons).

rubric.why: Identifies the three hydrogen isotopes and their mass numbers.
rubric.how: Award for naming or correctly symbolising protium, deuterium and tritium.

rubric.why: Identifies the common carbon isotopes by mass number.
rubric.how: Award for giving carbon-12, carbon-13 and carbon-14, with names or symbols.

rubric.why: Identifies the two common chlorine isotopes by mass number.
rubric.how: Award for giving chlorine-35 and chlorine-37, with names or symbols.

modelAnswer: Isotopes are atoms of the same element having the same atomic number but different mass numbers.
Hydrogen has three isotopes: protium (¹₁H), deuterium (²₁H) and tritium (³₁H).
Carbon has three common isotopes: carbon-12 (¹²₆C), carbon-13 (¹³₆C) and carbon-14 (¹⁴₆C).
Chlorine has two common isotopes: chlorine-35 (³⁵₁₇Cl) and chlorine-37 (³⁷₁₇Cl).

items.followUp: Describe how a coordinate covalent bond forms in the ammonium ion and the hydronium ion.

rubric.why: States that the shared electron pair comes from one atom.
rubric.description: Formation of a coordinate covalent bond
rubric.how: Award for explaining that one atom donates both electrons of the shared pair, typically from a lone pair, to an electron-deficient atom or ion.

rubric.why: Shows ammonia donating its lone pair to a hydrogen ion to form ammonium.
rubric.how: Award for the correct formation of NH₄⁺ from NH₃ and H⁺, including the coordinate bond from nitrogen to hydrogen.

rubric.why: Shows water donating a lone pair to a hydrogen ion to form hydronium.
rubric.how: Award for the correct formation of H₃O⁺ from H₂O and H⁺, including the coordinate bond from oxygen to hydrogen.

modelAnswer: A coordinate covalent bond is formed when one atom donates both electrons of a shared pair to another atom or ion.
In ammonia, nitrogen donates a lone pair to H⁺: NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺; the coordinate bond is shown by N→H.
In water, oxygen donates a lone pair to H⁺: H₂O + H⁺ → H₃O⁺; the coordinate bond is shown by O→H.
The atom donating the lone pair is the donor, and the atom or ion accepting it is the acceptor.

items.followUp: Define boiling point and explain how intermolecular forces affect it.

rubric.why: Defines vapour pressure in relation to a liquid and its vapour.
rubric.how: Award for stating that vapour pressure is the pressure exerted by a liquid's vapour, preferably when the vapour and liquid are in equilibrium in a closed container.

rubric.why: Connects intermolecular-force strength to how readily molecules escape into the vapour.
rubric.how: Award for explaining that stronger forces hold molecules in the liquid and lower vapour pressure, while weaker forces lead to higher vapour pressure.

modelAnswer: Vapour pressure is the pressure exerted by a vapour above its liquid when the vapour and liquid are in equilibrium in a closed container at a given temperature.
Strong intermolecular forces hold liquid molecules more tightly, so fewer escape into the vapour and the vapour pressure is lower.
Weak intermolecular forces allow more molecules to escape into the vapour, so the vapour pressure is higher.

items.followUp: Define solubility and state the general principle that helps predict whether a solute will dissolve in a solvent.

rubric.why: Includes the maximum amount of solute, saturation and the temperature condition.
rubric.how: Award for defining solubility as the maximum amount of solute that dissolves in a given amount of solvent to form a saturated solution at a specified temperature.

rubric.why: States the general solubility rule and its application to similar types of substances.
rubric.how: Award for stating “like dissolves like” and explaining that polar solutes tend to dissolve in polar solvents while non-polar solutes tend to dissolve in non-polar solvents.

modelAnswer: Solubility is the maximum amount of a solute that dissolves in a given amount of solvent to form a saturated solution at a specified temperature.
The general principle of solubility is “like dissolves like.”
Polar solutes generally dissolve in polar solvents, while non-polar solutes generally dissolve in non-polar solvents.

items.followUp: Name one use of uranium-235 in a nuclear power station.

rubric.why: Identifies a recognised use of uranium-235.
rubric.how: Award for stating that uranium-235 is used as fuel in nuclear reactors or in the manufacture of atomic weapons.

modelAnswer: Uranium-235 is used as fuel in nuclear reactors and in atomic bombs.

items.followUp: How many elements are present in the 2nd and 5th periods of the periodic table?

rubric.why: Gives the number of elements in the fourth period.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the fourth period contains 18 elements.

rubric.why: Gives the number of elements in the sixth period.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the sixth period contains 32 elements.

modelAnswer: The fourth period contains 18 elements.
The sixth period contains 32 elements.

items.followUp: Why does atomic radius decrease from left to right across a period?

rubric.why: Identifies the increase in occupied electron shells down a group.
rubric.how: Award for stating that each step down a group adds an electron shell or energy level.

rubric.why: Explains that the additional shell places the outer electrons farther from the nucleus.
rubric.how: Award for linking the added shells to the increased distance of the outer electrons from the nucleus and hence the larger atomic size.

modelAnswer: As we move down a group, each successive element has an additional electron shell.
The outer electrons are therefore farther from the nucleus, so the atomic size increases.
